newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian gamblers find Melbourne Cup a nightmare.
newsitem.headline: Australian gamblers find Melbourne Cup a nightmare.

text.p: Many Australians consider the Melbourne Cup horse race to be the highlight of their year, but for others, it can be a daytime nightmare.
Australia's second city ground to a halt on Tuesday and millions of people across the nation forgot their daily chores for "Cup Day" -- at least for three minutes and 18.8 seconds.
But for one group of Melbourne residents -- racing fans who can not control their urge to gamble -- it was the hardest afternoon of the year to get through.

"It can be a very stressful day for us, when so much is going on that involves gambling," said Marie, a volunteer with Gam-Anon, which tries to help compulsive gamblers live without the thrill of a punt.
In a telephone interview, Marie said that she and around 50 others were planning to gather in a Melbourne city park on Tuesday for a picnic and a game of cricket, no bets allowed.
Members of the group had been advised not to read the newspapers ahead of the big race -- which is given saturation coverage -- and to leave their radio switched off.
"But it's not just the race, it's all the other opportunities to gamble as well," explained Marie.

Australia is a nation of gamblers. On the horse racing front, the Melbourne Cup is the biggest day of the year with around A$80 million (US$62.3 million) bet with official bookmakers and millions more plunged in office sweepstakes and on the course itself.
Newspapers run countless pages on the pageantry of the Cup, its personalities and the odds punters are likely to be offered.
The biggest single bet this year was probably the A$1.0 million placed by Melbourne casino magnate Lloyd Williams, who bet A$1.0 million on last year's winner Doriemus.
Unfortunately for Williams, his horse finished sixth.
Countrywide, Australians and high-rolling visitors from Asia spend around A$50 billion on gambling every year.
An explosion in gambling in Australia in the past five years now sees all of the country's six states boasting casinos, as gambling provides a useful source of tax revenue.

Marie, a recovering gambling addict, said poker (slot) machines were among the biggest attractions. Studies have shown that "pokies", found in bars and even shopping malls, can swallow up more than two percent of family income.
"Some of us find ourselves in grave difficulty and find it difficult to live each day to its fullest," said Marie, oblivious to the fact that stayer Saintly had just won the Melbourne Cup.
